question: What makes a good pull request?
shortAnswer: Small focused scope, clear title/description explaining what and why, self-review before requesting reviewers, passing CI, linked issue, screenshots for UI changes — and prompt responses to feedback. Reviewers' time is the scarcest resource.
explanation: PR quality determines review speed. Scope: under ~400 changed lines review meaningfully; large features ship as stacked PRs or feature-flagged increments. Description answers three questions — what changed, why (link the ticket), how to verify (steps, test evidence) — with before/after screenshots for visual work. Self-review catches debug leftovers, stray formatting, and forces you to reread your own diff; it's also where you add comments guiding reviewers through tricky sections. Hygiene: branch rebased/current with main, CI green, no unrelated commits mixed in (that's what cherry-pick/rebase are for). During review, respond to every comment (even just 'done'), push follow-up commits rather than force-pushing mid-review so incremental diffs stay readable, then squash-merge per team convention. As reviewer: small PRs get thorough reviews within hours; giant ones get rubber-stamped within days — size is kindness.
example:
## What
Adds pagination to /api/orders (cursor-based).

## Why
Closes #482 — endpoint times out beyond ~5k orders.

## How tested
- Unit tests for cursor encoding
- Verified against 50k-row staging DB (screenshots)
- p95 latency: 1.2s → 140ms

## Note for reviewers
Cursor logic in `src/pagination.ts:40` is the subtle part.
interviewTip: Frame everything around reviewer efficiency, volunteer a concrete number (~400 lines), and show a mini description template — practical experience speaks loudest here.
commonMistakes: Giant mixed-concern PRs nobody reviews properly.
'Fixed' replies without pushed commits addressing feedback.

question: How do you resolve merge conflicts?
shortAnswer: Git marks conflicts with <<<<<<< / ======= / >>>>>>> markers. Open each file, decide the correct combined content, remove markers, git add, then continue the operation (rebase --continue/merge --continue). Understand both sides' intent — never blindly pick one.
explanation: Conflicts arise when two branches modify overlapping lines, or one deletes what another edits. Git pauses the integration, inserting four-part markers: yours above =======, theirs below, labeled by commit. Resolution means producing what the code *should* say given both intents — sometimes both changes, sometimes one superseding with knowledge of why. Tooling helps: VS Code's inline Accept Current/Mine/Theirs buttons, git meretool, or diff3 context (merge.conflictStyle diff3) showing the common ancestor for smarter judgment. After fixing each file: stage it, then continue — rebase replays remaining commits (later conflicts may recur), merge completes once. Abort cleanly anytime (git merge --abort / rebase --abort). Prevention matters more than cure: small frequent merges of main into long branches, coordinated module ownership, and communication when touching shared files reduce conflict frequency dramatically. Binary/generated files need explicit strategy (ours/theirs).
example:
<<<<<<< HEAD
const timeout = 5000;
=======
const timeout = 10_000;
>>>>>>> feature/configurable-timeout

// Resolved by understanding intent:
const timeout = Number(process.env.TIMEOUT_MS ?? 10_000);

git add config.js
git rebase --continue   # or merge --continue
interviewTip: Walk the marker anatomy fast, emphasize intent-understanding over side-picking, then close with prevention habits — that arc shows real team experience.
commonMistakes: Committing files with leftover conflict markers.
Not knowing --abort escapes cleanly.

question: What's the difference between clone, fork and branch?
shortAnswer: Branch is a movable pointer inside one repository — parallel lines of development. Clone downloads a repository to your machine with full history. Fork copies the repository to your own hosting account — used when you can't push to the original.
explanation: Three levels of isolation. Branches live *within* a repo: cheap pointers letting contributors share one remote while isolating work for review — the default team workflow. Clone brings a repo to local disk: full history, remotes configured; everyone clones regardless of access level. Fork duplicates the entire repository under your account on the platform — your copy, your permissions — connected to upstream via convention (git remote add upstream). Forks serve two audiences: external open-source contributors without write access (fork → clone fork → branch → push → PR upstream), and organizations needing experimentation space or security separation. Team members with write access skip forking entirely: clone canonical, push branches directly. Practical notes: sync forks via upstream fetch + main reset, or GitHub's 'Sync fork' button; keep origin/upstream naming consistent across teams; forks don't include issues/wiki/settings — they're code copies.
example:
# Open-source contribution flow:
git clone https://github.com/YOU/project.git
cd project
git remote add upstream https://github.com/ORIG/project.git
git checkout -b fix-typo
# ...commit...
git push origin fix-typo     # → open PR against upstream

# Team member flow:
git clone https://github.com/ORIG/project.git
git checkout -b feature-x && git push -u origin feature-x
interviewTip: Anchor each to permission levels — branch (same repo), clone (local copy), fork (hosting-level copy for no-write-access contributors). The OSS workflow demo seals it.
commonMistakes: Forking repos they already have write access to.
Not knowing forks lack issues/settings from upstream.

question: What is detached HEAD state and how does reflog save you?
shortAnswer: Detached HEAD means you checked out a commit instead of a branch — new commits aren't on any line and risk garbage collection. reflog records every HEAD movement (~90 days default), recovering 'lost' commits after resets, rebases or amends: git reset --hard <reflog-entry>.
explanation: HEAD normally points at a branch tip; checking out an arbitrary commit detaches it — fine for inspection, dangerous for work: commits made there belong to no branch, invisible in git log of any line, eventually collected. Recovery paths differ by goal: continuing work means creating a branch at that spot immediately (git switch -c new-branch); accidental detachment just needs returning to a named branch. The deeper lesson is reflog: Git journals every reference movement — checkouts, resets, amends, rebases — locally, keeping entries ~90 days. After a disastrous reset --hard or botched interactive rebase, git reflog shows the pre-mistake entry; restore via reset --hard HEAD@{n} or branch from it. This reframes Git psychology: almost nothing committed is ever truly lost — only unreferenced. Committed-but-never-added work (untracked/stashed carelessly dropped) has narrower recovery (fsck --lost-found). Share the mantra: reflog first, panic never.
example:
# Oops — hard reset lost three commits:
git reflog
# abc1234 HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to origin/main
# 8f3e21d HEAD@{1}: commit: add rate limiting   ← the one I want
# def5678 HEAD@{2}: commit: add retry logic

git reset --hard HEAD@{1}       # everything restored

# Or keep as a branch:
git branch rescue/feature 8f3e21d
interviewTip: Define detachment crisply, then perform a live reflog rescue narrative — 'nothing is lost' confidence is exactly what this question tests.
commonMistakes: Thinking reset --hard permanently deletes commits.
Committing extensively while detached without branching.

question: What are conventional commits and how do they connect to versioning?
shortAnswer: Conventional commits structure messages as type(scope): description — feat, fix, docs, refactor, test, chore. Types drive semantic versioning automatically: feat bumps minor, fix bumps patch, breaking changes (feat!:/BREAKING CHANGE) bump major — tools like semantic-release automate releases and changelogs from history.
explanation: Standardized messages turn commit history into machine-readable release data. Format: type(optional scope): imperative description — feat(auth): add OAuth login. Core types: feat (new capability), fix (bug), plus non-release-affecting docs/refactor/perf/test/build/chore/ci. Breaking changes signal two ways: exclamation feat!:(api): ... or a BREAKING CHANGE: footer paragraph — both trigger major bumps. The payoff chain: semantic-version tooling reads commits since last tag, computes next version (patch/minor/major), generates changelogs grouped by type, tags and publishes — semantic-release/release-please run this hands-free in CI. Benefits compound: reviewers scan type prefixes for relevance, git log --grep='fix' filters bug timelines, generated changelogs stay accurate without manual curation. Enforcement ranges from commit-msg hooks (commitlint + husky) squashing mistakes early, to squash-merge conventions where the PR title becomes the commit — making well-formed titles a team habit rather than a plugin mandate.
example:
feat(checkout): support Apple Pay
fix(api): handle empty cart 400s        # → patch bump
docs: update setup guide                # no release
refactor!: drop Node 16 support         # → major bump

BREAKING CHANGE: /v1/orders removed; use /v2/orders.

# Automated pipeline:
commits since v2.3.0 → feat+fix detected → release v2.4.0 + changelog
interviewTip: Recite format + the version-bump mapping table quickly, then name semantic-release automation — connecting messages to pipelines shows systems thinking beyond etiquette.
commonMistakes: Mixing up which types trigger which version bumps.
Forgetting BREAKING CHANGE footers exist alongside the ! shorthand.

question: What are Git hooks and how do teams use them to enforce quality?
shortAnswer: Git hooks are scripts Git runs automatically at key points — pre-commit (lint/format before a commit lands), commit-msg (enforce message conventions), pre-push (run tests before sharing). They live in `.git/hooks/` so they are not cloned; teams share them via a hooksPath config or tools like Husky to keep standards consistent across machines.
explanation: Hooks are executable scripts named after lifecycle events, stored in `.git/hooks/` — Git runs them when the matching event fires and blocks the action if they exit non-zero. Practical pairings: pre-commit runs linters/formatters (ESLint, Prettier) so bad code never reaches the index; commit-msg validates message format (enforcing Conventional Commits) and rejects malformed ones; pre-push runs the test suite locally before the network round-trip. post-checkout can install dependencies after a branch switch. The catch: `.git/hooks/` is not versioned, so a fresh clone starts empty. Teams solve this three ways — a `core.hooksPath` pointing to a tracked `hooks/` directory, a prepare/install script that copies them, or Husky (which writes a tiny shim per hook and declares hooks in package.json). Combine with CI as the real gatekeeper — hooks are a fast local convenience, not a security boundary, since any developer can `git commit --no-verify`. Use them to save time and catch trivial mistakes, not to replace server-side checks.
example:
# Husky (declared in package.json) — shared via repo:
# .husky/pre-commit
#!/bin/sh
. "$(dirname "$0")/_/husky.sh"
npx lint-staged

# .husky/commit-msg
#!/bin/sh
. "$(dirname "$0")/_/husky.sh"
npx --no -- commitlint --edit ${1}

# Track hooks without Husky (git config):
git config core.hooksPath ./hooks
interviewTip: List the three most useful hooks (pre-commit, commit-msg, pre-push) with concrete tools, then address the sharing problem — that is what separates book knowledge from team experience.
commonMistakes: Forgetting hooks are local and not shared on clone.
Treating hooks as a security boundary instead of a convenience.
Forgetting developers can bypass with --no-verify.

question: What is the difference between a lightweight tag and an annotated tag, and which should you use for releases?
shortAnswer: A lightweight tag is just a named pointer to a commit — a bookmark. An annotated tag is a full Git object storing a message, the tagger name and email, and the date. Use annotated tags for releases: they are checksummed, carry release notes, can be signed with GPG, and tools like `git describe` and release automation rely on them.
explanation: `git tag v1.2.0` creates a lightweight tag — a ref in `refs/tags/` pointing at a commit, with no metadata. `git tag -a v1.2.0 -m 'Release notes'` creates an annotated tag, a real object with author, date, and message. The practical differences: `git show` on an annotated tag displays the message; `git tag -v` can verify a GCP signature (only possible on annotated tags); `git describe` prefers annotated tags when computing version strings; and release tooling (semantic-release, GitHub Release automation) reads annotated tag messages to build changelogs. Lightweight tags suit private bookmarks; annotated tags are the standard for anything published. For releases, go further: sign with `git tag -s` (or `-u <key>`) so consumers can verify provenance, and push tags explicitly (`git push --tags` or better, push the release tag only). Tag the merge commit on main, not a feature-branch commit, so the tag reflects what shipped.
example:
# Annotated release tag with message:
git tag -a v1.2.0 -m 'v1.2.0 — cursor pagination, export CSV'

# Signed tag (verifiable provenance):
git tag -s v1.2.0 -m 'v1.2.0 release'
git tag -v v1.2.0            # verify signature

# Push the release tag:
git push origin v1.2.0

# Release automation reads it:
git describe --tags          # => v1.2.0
interviewTip: Give the bookmark-versus-object distinction, then immediately say 'annotated for releases' and list why — message, GPG signing, git describe, and changelog tooling. One line each.
commonMistakes: Using lightweight tags for releases and losing metadata.
Forgetting to push tags — commits go with `git push`, tags need `git push --tags`.
Tagging a feature-branch commit instead of the merge commit on main.

question: Compare GitFlow, GitHub Flow and trunk-based development. When does each make sense?
shortAnswer: GitFlow uses long-lived branches (develop, feature, release, hotfix) with formal merges — structured but heavy, suited to scheduled releases and multiple supported versions. GitHub Flow is minimal: main is always deployable, short-lived feature branches merged via PR — ideal for continuous deployment. Trunk-based goes further: developers integrate into main at least daily via tiny short-lived branches, relying on feature flags instead of long branches.
explanation: GitFlow (Vincent Driessen) models the full release lifecycle: `develop` integrates features, `release/*` branches stabilize, `hotfix/*` patches production, all merging back to both `main` and `develop`. It shines when you ship on a cadence and maintain several production versions, but the branch overhead and merge churn are real costs. GitHub Flow strips it down: `main` is sacred and always deployable; every change is a feature branch opened, reviewed via PR, CI-passed, then merged and deployed. Perfect for web apps deploying many times a day. Trunk-based development pushes integration frequency further — developers merge to `main` at least daily, using branches that live hours not days, and hide incomplete work behind feature flags rather than long-lived branches. It minimizes merge debt and suits high-velocity teams with strong CI and flag infrastructure. Choosing: regulated/multi-version software leans GitFlow; most SaaS products fit GitHub Flow; elite-velocity teams with mature CI adopt trunk-based. The common thread — pick the simplest model that matches your release cadence and tooling, then enforce it with branch protection and CI.
example:
# GitHub Flow (most web apps):
# main always deployable → feature branch → PR → review → merge → deploy

# Trunk-based (high velocity):
# branch lives < 1 day → PR → merge to main → feature flag gates the UI

# GitFlow (scheduled releases):
# develop ← feature/* → release/* → main + hotfix/*
interviewTip: Map each model to a release cadence (continuous / daily / scheduled) and name feature flags as the enabler for trunk-based. That decision framework is what interviewers want, not just definitions.
commonMistakes: Adopting GitFlow for a simple web app and drowning in branches.
Doing trunk-based without feature flags, shipping half-finished work.
Treating the workflow as dogma instead of matching it to release cadence.

question: What are signed commits and why would a team require them?
shortAnswer: Signed commits are cryptographically verified with GPG or SSH, proving a trusted author made them. A team requires them so every merged commit is attributable and tamper-evident — GitHub shows a Verified badge and can block unsigned commits via branch protection.
explanation: By default a commit's author field is free text — anyone can claim to be `Alice <alice@example.com>`. Signing attaches a cryptographic signature: `git commit -S` signs with a GPG key (or SSH key via `git commit -S` with `gpg.format = ssh`). Git stores the signature in the commit object; anyone with the public key can verify it with `git verify-commit`. GitHub checks signatures and shows Verified/Unverified badges on commits and tags. Why enforce it: it ties every change to a real identity, deterring impersonation and making the audit trail trustworthy — important in regulated or security-sensitive projects. Enforcement options: branch protection rules requiring signed commits (GitHub Enterprise), CI checks that reject unsigned commits, or pre-receive hooks. Practical setup: generate a GPG key (`gpg --full-generate-key`), add it to your GitHub account, tell Git your signing key (`git config user.signingkey`), and enable commit signing globally (`git config commit.gpgsign true`) or per-repo. SSH signing is simpler to onboard (reuses existing SSH keys) and is now a first-class alternative. The trade-off: key management overhead and a harder onboarding for new contributors.
example:
# Configure GPG signing:
gpg --full-generate-key
gpg --list-secret-keys --keyid-format=long
git config --global user.signingkey <KEYID>
git config --global commit.gpgsign true

# Sign a commit:
git commit -S -m 'feat: add export'

# Verify locally:
git verify-commit HEAD

# SSH signing (simpler onboarding):
git config gpg.format ssh
git config user.signingkey ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
interviewTip: Lead with the impersonation problem (author field is free text), then explain GPG/SSH signing and how GitHub surfaces it. Mentioning branch protection enforcement shows you have seen it required, not just read about it.
commonMistakes: Thinking the author field is verified — it is free text without signing.
Signing commits but never configuring verification on the server side.
Overlooking SSH signing as a simpler alternative to GPG.

question: What happens when you commit large binary files to Git, and how should you handle them instead?
shortAnswer: Git stores a full copy of every version of every file, so large binaries bloat the repo permanently — clones slow down and history stays heavy even after you delete the file. Use Git LFS to store pointer files in the repo and the real binaries on a remote server, keeping clone size and history lean.
explanation: Git snapshots each file per commit. A 100 MB binary changed ten times adds a gigabyte to history; deleting it later does not help — the old versions remain in the object database, so every clone still downloads them. Large File Storage (Git LFS) replaces tracked large files with tiny pointer files in the repo and uploads the real objects to an LFS server (GitHub LFS, GitLab, or self-hosted). Setup: `git lfs install` once per machine, then `git lfs track '*.psd' '*.zip'` to register patterns (this writes `.gitattributes`), commit the `.gitattributes` file, and work normally — checkout and push pull the real files transparently. LFS servers have storage and bandwidth quotas (GitHub: 1 GB free storage + 1 GB/month bandwidth on the free tier), so teams sometimes self-host or cap tracked file sizes. For binaries already in history, migrate with `git lfs migrate import --include='*.psd'` (rewrites history, so coordinate with the team) or prune with `git filter-repo` / BFG. Prevention: enforce file-size limits with a pre-commit or pre-receive hook and document which patterns belong in LFS in the README. Alternatives worth naming: Git Annex for fully distributed binary management, or simply keeping large assets out of version control entirely (CDN + versioned URLs) when history is not needed.
example:
# Install and configure LFS:
git lfs install
git lfs track '*.psd' '*.mp4' '*.zip'
git add .gitattributes
git commit -m 'chore: track binaries with LFS'

# Work normally — LFS handles the rest:
git add design.psd
git push origin main

# Migrate existing binaries into LFS (history rewrite):
git lfs migrate import --include='*.psd' --everything
interviewTip: Lead with the permanent-bloat problem (deleting does not shrink history), then present LFS as the fix and mention quotas and the `.gitattributes` file. Naming the migration command shows you have dealt with the mess after the fact.
commonMistakes: Deleting a large file and expecting the repo to shrink.
Forgetting to commit .gitattributes so LFS patterns are not shared.
Not accounting for LFS storage and bandwidth quotas on the chosen host.
